To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the five most common serogroups/types in our study (6, 14,9,19 and 23) were the same in each year and that the nonavalent conjugate vaccine would cover 74% of blood and cerebrospinial fluid isolates and over 90% of the antibiotic resistant isolates.

serogroups/types 6, 9V, 14, and 19F, and 23F occurred most commonly in all three years of the study, and that the nonavalent conjugate pneumococcal vaccines offer the best protection against the serotypes most commonly encountered.

the five most commonly occurring serogroups/types in the UK were 6, 9 and 14, 6 and 14 being the most common serogroup in each year of study; 51% of isolates belonged to the 7-valent conjugate vaccine, 75% to the 9-valent, and 96% to the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine; 74% of blood and CSF isolates, and 90% antibiotic resistant
In summary, our research is concerned with
the serogroups/types and susceptibility to antimicrobial drugs of Streptococcal pneumoniae isolates in the United Kingdom.
the serogroups/types and the antibiotic resistance of referred strains of Streptocococcus pneumoniae.
the prevalence of serogroups/types and their resistance to antibiotics of Streptococus pneumoniae in the United Kingdom.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the serogrouping and serotyping of isolates of S pneumoniae from blood and cerebro-spinal fluid is a useful adjunct to antibiotic susceptibility testing in the clinical laboratory.
the nonavalent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine would be the most appropriate vaccine to use in the UK, and that the 23-valent vaccine is less useful.
the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is the least useful of the currently available vaccines in the United Kingdom.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
serogroup 14 was the most commonly isolated serogroup over the period 1993-1995 and serogroup 6 was the second most common serogroup.

the nonavalent conjugate vaccine is the most promising vaccine for the prevention of pneumococcus infection in the UK, and that this vaccine is likely to provide protection against most antibiotic resistant strains of S. pneumonia.
the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine is effective against the majority of pneumococci, but that conjugate vaccines would be more effective.
The main takeaway from our work is that

serogrouping or serotyping of isolates is a useful adjunct to susceptibility testing, and that the prevalence of the serogroup or serotype in the population is important when assessing the clinical significance of an isolate.
the conjugate nonavalent vaccine has potential for use as an empirical therapy in the UK.
the conjugate nonavalent vaccine is a good candidate for the next pneumococcal conjugate vaccine.
